claims.text: Every page on sgit.ai now has a price of a few pence, and a meter in the corner of the screen debits it from five pounds of starting credit.
claims.quote: Every page on sgit.ai now has a price, a few pence

claims.text: All of it lives in the reader's browser and nowhere else: no account, no server, no card, nothing sent.
claims.quote: no account, no server, no card, nothing sent

claims.text: A private window restarts the meter at five pounds, but also with no history, and the history is what the site uses to pick articles for the reader.
claims.quote: it also starts again with no history, and the history is what the site uses to pick articles for you

claims.text: Whether people would make the trade, pay a little, keep the record on their own machine and get a site that knows them back, is the question worth testing.
claims.quote: Whether people would make that trade is the question worth testing

claims.text: The meter has since gone live: it charges by how much of a page you read, the balance can go below zero with nothing blocked, a page can be declined with a reason, and topping up is a £5 Stripe payment.
claims.quote: it charges by how much of a page you read, your balance can go below zero with nothing blocked

claims.text: In the live version prices rose to 10p and 5p for articles.
claims.quote: Prices rose to 10p and 5p for articles.

value.unit: pence for a recent article in the live meter

claims.text: In the first version an article published in the last seven days costs 5p, an older one 3p, a newsletter issue, desk note or collection 2p, any other page 1p, and the homepage is free.
claims.quote: An article published in the last seven days costs 5p, an older one 3p

value.unit: pence for an article published in the last seven days

claims.text: The reader starts with £5.00 of credit, each page is debited once per visit, and going back to a page in the same session costs nothing.
claims.quote: and each page you open is debited once per visit

claims.text: Out of credit nothing is blocked: the page is shown, the read is recorded as unpaid, and a bar offers a top-up.
claims.quote: The page is shown, the read is recorded as unpaid, and a bar offers a top-up.

claims.text: Topping up has every step of a real shop except the payment: four packs, a cart, a review step, a confirm button and a receipt.
claims.quote: has every step of a real shop except the payment

claims.text: The list of what you read, with topics, is enough to personalise the site: the account and the front page pick unread articles from the topics read most, in a Picked for you band.
claims.quote: That list is enough to personalise the site.

claims.text: The browser does the arithmetic from the published articles/graphs.json, and the history never leaves the machine it was made on.
claims.quote: The history never leaves the machine it was made on.

claims.text: The meter can be escaped but the personalisation cannot be copied; the experiment is whether a site that knows what you read makes a few pence a page feel fair.
claims.quote: The meter can be escaped; the personalisation cannot be copied.

claims.text: A meter that charges nothing is the cheapest honest way to ask the question: price it, show the price, and give it away to people who know you.
claims.quote: Because it is the cheapest honest way to ask the question.

claims.text: The idea is old, 402 Payment Required was reserved in 1997; this meter asks whether the interesting part is the payment at all or what the reader gets back for the record of having paid.
claims.quote: whether the interesting part is the payment at all, or what the reader gets back for the record of having paid

claims.text: The first version was on the Portuguese newsroom: one cent a page, a five-euro wallet that refills itself, and a ledger page of its own.
claims.quote: one cent a page, a five-euro wallet that refills itself when it empties

claims.text: The Portuguese rules are kept: say it is a demonstration, never block a page, charge once per page per visit, and work if the browser refuses to store anything.
claims.quote: never block a page, charge once per page per visit so the back button is not a purchase

claims.text: Prices depend on what a page is and how new it is, set in one place in the site's build so the published table and the meter cannot disagree.
claims.quote: set in one place in the site's build so the published table and the meter cannot disagree

claims.text: The meter holds no money; anybody can edit their balance in developer tools, and real money would need a server or receipts signed by one.
claims.quote: Anybody can edit their own balance in the browser's developer tools.

claims.text: It does not follow the reader between devices; the history stays where it was made.
claims.quote: The history stays where it was made.

claims.text: A version that syncs could keep the ledger in an encrypted vault only the reader holds the key to; that is a proposal, not something built.
claims.quote: that is a proposal, not something built

claims.text: It does not meter agents: reading a page's markdown twin or the newsroom's wire costs nothing.
claims.quote: It does not meter agents.

claims.text: It charges the same for every reader; the obvious next prices are per question rather than per page.
claims.quote: The obvious next prices are not per page but per question

claims.text: The article was drafted from a voice note by Dinis Cruz by a Claude Code session working as the newsroom on 10 October 2026; the meter is assets/meter.js.
claims.quote: by a Claude Code session working as the sgit.ai newsroom, on 10 October 2026
